person.name: Benjamin_Franklin
person.tagline: Lightning Rods for an Independent America
person.summary: Benjamin Franklin was a Philadelphia printer, writer, inventor, scientist, civic organizer, and public official. His experiments with electricity produced the lightning rod and helped establish his scientific reputation. He became a leading advocate for American independence and secured French support during the Revolutionary War.

conclusion: Lightning rods still protect buildings and ships by directing electrical charge safely to the ground. Poor Richard's Almanack remains one of Franklin's best-known publications. The Declaration of Independence remains a central document in United States history. The postal network Franklin organized connected the colonies and later developed into a national system.

events.title: Born into a Boston Artisan Household
events.description: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston to Josiah Franklin, a tallow chandler and soapmaker, and Abiah Folger Franklin. He was their eighth child and Josiah's fifteenth child. The family lived within Boston's Congregational community, and Franklin was baptized at Old South Meeting House.

events.title: Begins a Printing Apprenticeship
events.description: At 12, Benjamin Franklin left school after two years because his family could not afford further education. In Boston, Josiah Franklin apprenticed him to his older brother James Franklin, a printer. Franklin learned typesetting, printing, and newspaper work in James's shop.

images.caption: James Franklin's Ramage printing press
images.creator: Justin Winsor, Illustration by unknown artist

events.title: Runs to Philadelphia
events.description: In October 1723, Benjamin Franklin left Boston after quarreling with his brother James over his restrictive printing apprenticeship. He traveled alone to Philadelphia, where he sought work as a printer and a new start.
events.background:
James’s 1722 imprisonment had briefly put Benjamin in charge of the New-England Courant. Benjamin used the paper to continue the Silence Dogood letters that had become a subject of conversation in Boston. James reacted badly after learning that his younger brother had written them.

The terms of the apprenticeship gave Benjamin no authorized way to leave. His departure made him a fugitive. In Philadelphia, he found employment in several printing shops. The work did not offer prospects he found satisfactory.

background_images.caption: Benjamin Franklin editorial in the New-England Courant, July 16-23, 1722 issue
background_images.creator: Benjamin Franklin editorial in the New-England Courant, July 16-23, 1722 issue

events.title: Returns to Philadelphia from London
events.description: Governor William Keith had promised support for a Philadelphia newspaper and failed to provide it. Benjamin Franklin worked as a typesetter in London. In 1726, English merchant Thomas Denham brought Franklin back to Philadelphia and employed him in his business.

events.title: Acquires The Pennsylvania Gazette
events.description: In 1729, Benjamin Franklin and Hugh Meredith acquired The Pennsylvania Gazette, a Philadelphia newspaper, from printer Samuel Keimer. The partners had established their printing business the year before. Franklin used the paper for news, essays, satire, and arguments for local reforms.

events.title: Forms a Household with Deborah Read
events.description: In 1730, Benjamin Franklin and Deborah Read began living publicly as husband and wife in Philadelphia. Read's first husband, John Rogers, had deserted her. Because his death could not be proved, Franklin and Read entered a common-law marriage.

events.title: Publishes Poor Richard's Almanack
events.description: In 1732, Benjamin Franklin began publishing Poor Richard's Almanack, an annual almanac, under the pseudonym Richard Saunders. He filled it with calendars, practical information, humor, and sayings for colonial readers. It sold about 10,000 copies a year.

event_class.title: Poor Richard's Almanack
event_class.impact: It sold about 10,000 copies a year and became one of colonial America's most widely read publications.

events.title: Tests Lightning's Electrical Nature
events.description: In Philadelphia in 1752, Benjamin Franklin investigated whether lightning carried electrical charge. His experiments established that lightning and electricity were the same force. Franklin developed the lightning rod to protect buildings from lightning strikes.

event_class.title: Lightning rod
event_class.description: A pointed metal rod connects a building to the ground and directs electrical charge away from its structure.
event_class.impact: Lightning rods became a standard means of protecting buildings and ships from lightning strikes.

events.background:
Franklin’s electrical work grew from experiments undertaken with apparatus sent by Peter Collinson, a London merchant and fellow of the Royal Society. Ebenezer Kinnersley joined him in Philadelphia. Franklin described the results in a series of letters to Collinson. Collinson gathered them into Experiments and Observations on Electricity Made at Philadelphia in America in 1751. The book circulated in Europe and was translated into several languages.

A proposal in Franklin’s correspondence called for collecting electrical effects from a storm cloud. Thomas-François Dalibard conducted such an experiment at Marly-la-Ville, France, in May 1752. The Royal Society awarded Franklin the Copley Medal in 1753 for his experiments and observations on electricity.

events.title: Oversees the Colonial Post
events.description: In 1753, Benjamin Franklin and William Hunter became deputy postmasters-general for British North America. They supervised the mail service across the colonies. Franklin improved postal accounting and delivery routes between Philadelphia, New York, and Boston.

events.title: Becomes Pennsylvania's London Agent
events.description: In 1757, the Pennsylvania Assembly sent Benjamin Franklin to London as its colonial agent. He argued against the political privileges of the [[Penn family proprietors]], who owned Pennsylvania. Franklin presented the assembly's case to British officials.

Penn family proprietors.explanation: The Penn family held proprietary control of Pennsylvania under a grant from the English Crown. Their political privileges and tax exemptions were a source of conflict with the colony's assembly.

events.title: Testifies Against the Stamp Act
events.description: In February 1766, Benjamin Franklin testified before the House of Commons, the lower house of the British Parliament. The 1765 Stamp Act required stamped paper for legal documents, newspapers, and other printed materials. Franklin told members that the colonies opposed the tax, and Parliament repealed it on March 18.

images.caption: House of Commons chamber in London
images.creator: UK Parliament

events.title: Helps Draft Independence Declaration
events.description: In Philadelphia, Benjamin Franklin joined Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Roger Sherman, and Robert Livingston on the five-member committee that drafted the [[Declaration of Independence]]. The committee prepared the text for the [[Continental Congress]], the representative body of the colonies. Franklin helped revise Jefferson's draft before Congress adopted it on July 4, 1776.

images.caption: John Trumbull's Declaration of Independence painting
images.creator: John Trumbull

Declaration of Independence.explanation: The document in which the thirteen colonies announced their separation from Great Britain. The Continental Congress adopted it on July 4, 1776.

Continental Congress.explanation: The representative body that coordinated resistance to Great Britain and served as the revolutionary government. Its Second Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence.

events.background:
Richard Henry Lee's June 7 resolution for independence prompted Congress to appoint the drafting committee four days later. Jefferson wrote the first draft while staying at Jacob Graff Jr.'s Philadelphia house. He then gave it to Franklin and Adams for their edits before the committee submitted a proposed text on June 28.

Franklin made one of the best-known revisions to Jefferson's wording. He replaced the phrase “sacred and undeniable” with “self-evident” in the assertion about human equality and rights.

Congress considered the committee's text over four days. Its delegates made additional changes, including cutting a passage that blamed the British Crown for the slave trade and for encouraging enslaved people to seek freedom through revolt.

events.title: Signs the French Alliance Treaties
events.description: On February 6, 1778, Benjamin Franklin, Arthur Lee, and Silas Deane signed the Treaty of Amity and Commerce in Paris. The treaty established commercial relations between France and the United States. They also signed the Treaty of Alliance, which committed France to military cooperation against Britain.

events.title: Signs Treaty of Paris
events.description: Benjamin Franklin signed the [[Treaty of Paris|Treaty of Paris]] in Paris with John Adams and John Jay on September 3, 1783. The agreement recognized the independence of the United States and formally ended the American Revolutionary War.

images.caption: First page of the 1783 Treaty of Paris

Treaty of Paris.explanation: The Treaty of Paris was the peace agreement between Great Britain and the United States that concluded the American Revolutionary War. It recognized American independence and established the new nation's boundaries.

events.title: Becomes President of Pennsylvania
events.description: In 1785, Benjamin Franklin returned to Philadelphia and became President of Pennsylvania. The office made him the state's chief executive.

images.caption: Benjamin Franklin signed check as Pennsylvania president
images.creator: National Museum of American History

events.title: Dies at Home in Philadelphia
events.description: Benjamin Franklin died at his Philadelphia home after suffering from [[pleurisy]]. In his final years, he lived with his daughter Sarah Franklin Bache, her husband Richard Bache, and their family.

pleurisy.explanation: Pleurisy is inflammation of the tissues surrounding the lungs, often causing sharp chest pain and difficult breathing.
